items.title: What Google and Reddit's bad days have in common
items.text:
What Google and Reddit's bad days have in common
This is a column about AI. My fiancé works at Anthropic. See my full ethics disclosure here.On Thursday afternoon, Demis Hassabis celebrated a milestone for Google’s AI efforts: Gemini 4 Carbon, a new large language model that is currently available only to cyber defenders, topped Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index. After a series of delays in new model releases and a growing perception that the company is falling off the frontier, early signs suggest that Carbon marks a return to form. For Alphabet’s chief scientist, the news surely felt like a vindication. Investors, however, are much less certain. On the same day, Google’s parent company had its worst day in history as a public company. Alphabet’s stock fell 12.6 percent, erasing around $500 billion in market value. The loss marked the second-biggest stock market plunge ever, following Nvidia’s $593 billion slide in January 2025. And it was Google’s biggest one-day decline since the great financial crisis.Most of the selloff came from investor worries about the huge scale of Google’s AI infrastructure buildout. The company plans to spend up to $205 billion on capital expenses

items.title: API credits benefit for eligible ChatGPT subscriptions
items.text:
API credits benefit for eligible ChatGPT subscriptions
API credits benefit for eligible ChatGPT subscriptions Earlier this month Anthropic announced a generous new benefit for their Max and Team subscriptions: $100, $200, and $500 per month subscribers would get the equivalent quantity of (expiring) credits to use with the Anthropic API. OpenAI have now launched pretty much exactly the same deal: if you have a $100, $200, or $500 subscription plan with them you now get that same quantity of credits to apply to one of your API organizations. I maintain subscriptions with both companies, so this is great news for me! I may even ship some public-facing demos now that the credits are already covered by my existing subscriptions. items.text:
Nvidia Moves to Backstop a Cloud Provider’s $45 Billion Anthropic Project
Nvidia is in talks to provide Nscale, a young AI cloud provider, with billions of dollars in credit guarantees for debt to develop a 460-megawatt data center that Anthropic plans to use, according to people with knowledge of the deal discussions. The deal is not yet signed, and terms could change. But it is another example of how Nvidia has continued to signal its financial support of so-called neoclouds like Nscale, CoreWeave and Firmus, which have faced pressure from investors because of the debt those companies have raised and will still need to raise to develop specialized data centers for AI.

‘Skeptical’ Lawyers Highlight Growing Pains of AI Agents
As Anthropic correctly pointed out in its initial public offering filing, business use of AI is in its infancy. Many other corporate executives say it will take some time for white-collar workers, especially those who aren’t software engineers, to use the latest tools effectively.For example, White & Case, a large global law firm with more than 2,000 lawyers, is “having to hold back” its rollout of one of the newest legal assistants made by AI startup Legora because lawyers are hesitant about using so-called AI agents, said Isabel Parker, the law firm’s chief innovation officer. A gradual rollout will ensure lawyers feel confident in using the new agent, which can handle more complex legal work than the AI agent from Legora that lawyers currently use for tasks such as analyzing and summarizing documents and generating ideas, she said. Unlike simpler chatbots, AI agents can take multiple actions on behalf of the user.Lawyers “are not the kind of people that easily lend themselves to using AI,” she told The Information’s Laura Mandaro during the WTF Summit, a gathering of senior women leaders in tech and finance. items.title: Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models
items.text:
Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models
How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models. Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world. I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle. By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens per month ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens"). Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request. Savi files bugs herself. items.title: Encryption Under Siege? OpenAI, Anthropic Disprove Key Cryptography Theorem
items.text:
Encryption Under Siege? OpenAI, Anthropic Disprove Key Cryptography Theorem
Cryptographers who develop encryption technologies may not be sleeping very well these days.OpenAI and Anthropic both said Monday that their internal AI models had disproven the Exponential Time Hypothesis, a longstanding computer science theorem that predicts the minimum difficulty of solving a certain category of problems. Cryptographers had long assumed the hypothesis was true, and built other findings on the basis of that assumption.Disproving the Exponential Time Hypothesis won’t endanger any current encryption methods, said Matthew Green, professor of computer science at Johns Hopkins University and founder of encryption startup Zeutro. But the finding is a big theoretical step, showing that some problems are easier to solve than cryptographers had thought.That means cryptographers could also be wrong about other assumptions underlying core encryption methods such as elliptic curve encryption, a method underlying the majority of internet traffic, which would create a scramble to find new ways to keep information on the internet secure.

The S-1 document published earlier this week is hundreds upon hundreds of pages filled with details that finally paint a picture of the economics of a frontier AI lab. As you might imagine, that picture is both really complicated and built on a series of very, very ambitious assumptions about the future and what AI will do to it. So I wanted to have Joey on the show to help break down what this document tells us, both about Anthropic’s finances and the broader AI economy. items.author: The Algorithmic Bridge
items.title: New Study: Anthropic Just Gave You a Reason to Stop Working With AI
items.text:
New Study: Anthropic Just Gave You a Reason to Stop Working With AI
Pick the number you think is the best between 1 and 10. Ready? Keep it in your head. Now open an AI chatbot, it doesn’t matter which—you can try a few if you want—and ask it the exact same thing. Done? Odds are, it picked number 7.We know this happens, and it’s not a mystery why: In part, it’s because humans overwhelmingly prefer 7 and it’s present a lot in the training data, etc. But, more importantly, the natural variation of human choice disappears inside AI due to a phenomenon known as “mode collapse.” AI concentrates its outputs around a narrow subset of possible answers, neglecting alternatives. It’s particularly striking and pervasive with numbers between 1 and 10, but it happens in general.Let’s try once more: pick the best writer ever, only one name. Hold on to it and ask your preferred AI the same thing. Shakespeare will win most of the time. Same reason. One last time: favorite color. At this point you will surely try to avoid the obvious choice—blue, which wins in most countries—but AI doesn’t bother with humans’ universal need for uniqueness. It will pick blue more than 90% of the time regardless.YouGo

Show HN: Nouli – A multi-turn decision graph harness for System One models
I've been fine tuning my own decision models lately and I've been interested in how there are no real multi-turn harnesses out there for decision models. I decided to build my own. The standard claude code style interface doesn't quite make sense with a decision model since it isn't a conversation so I built this out as a sort-of REPL inspired interface. You can also use it with the command line.You just type facts as you get them and ask questions with a ?. The questions stick around so every new fact gets asked again and you can see the probabilities move. You can use this to chain together different series of decisions to power decision networks and graphs with nouli. What Wall Street Really Thinks About the AI Trade Now
It has been a big week for the AI trade — we've seen wobbles in the market, many of them in response to headlines like the Anthropic S-1 and earnings from the hyperscalers (Oracle, Microsoft, etc.). So what does Wall Street make of all the news, and how are they processing an increasing sense that the laws of the economy barely apply to AI? Today, we speak with Alexander 'Alty' Altmann, global head of equities tactical strategies at Barclays, and he helps us make sense of how Wall Street really feels about the AI trade right now. We also talk about the KOSPI-fication of the S&P 500, if there are any historical precedents for the capex going into the AI buildout, and if AI is really immune to interest rates. items.title: OpenAI’s Astra Model Becomes Top Distillation Target for China’s AI Labs
items.text:
OpenAI’s Astra Model Becomes Top Distillation Target for China’s AI Labs
OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, the most powerful model the company has released, has met with strong demand since its release in early September. One growing customer base: Chinese AI labs that look to extract Astra’s capabilities. DeepSeek and Moonshot AI, two of China’s leading AI developers, relied heavily on outputs from Astra when training their own latest models, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter. The practice, known in the industry as distillation, continues to be one of the biggest contributors to the progress made by Chinese open-weight models despite repeated criticism of such efforts by OpenAI and rival Anthropic.

I burned about $500 for this fun project: Small Python. Initial PoC used 3 resets of Codex in one session but all later development happens in Claude Code, also in one Opus 5.5 session over three days.The outcome is a quickjs-like implementation for Python. Almost full Python 3.15 language features plus builtins are covered. No Lib/ support. Great for embedding scenarios.No rust. Just plain C11 code.Repo is here: https://github.com/soasme/small-python/Ask me anything.

items.author: Latent Space
items.title: Why Agents Love Supabase
items.text:
Why Agents Love Supabase
I first met Paul Copplestone and Ant Wilson in Singapore, shortly after they finished YC as the hottest startup of YC S20. Six years later, we finally got them on the podcast! This is their first podcast together, after taking an open-source, fully remote company from zero to a $10 billion valuation. The title is a question I wanted to understand for myself: why do agents love Supabase? There are plenty of managed databases. Postgres hosting is competitive. Being familiar to a model is useful distribution, but it doesn't explain all the work needed to turn a generated application into something that runs. But when I ran my frontier AEO tracker, it was an almost complete sweep of first choice for app backends (and in contention for managed db) for every frontier model from Astra to Fable to Muse. At Select, Supabase grouped its announcements into Build, Operate and Scale. The things that stood out to me were surprisingly practical: start a local backend without Docker, keep the desired database schema in Git, and run compute beside the database. Each removes a piece of work that developers have been doing for years. Agents make that friction harder to ignore

The October inflection point for vibe game development
I've written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents - the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we've reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it's for vibe coding computer games. Tree Appreciator Emberwick Battle Drones Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove Four times as insulting What happens if someone actually puts the work in? You should build a game! Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game: 3D modeling Music generation (see Scrimshaw Jukebox) Game design (!) That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments. The challenge has been getting to a game that's actually fun to play. Game design is a deep subject area. I won't pretend to be well versed in it - I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. The full text is finally here, so we are giving it the full RTFB of model card treatment. First, a recap of the state of Anthropic finances, then a close reading of the relevant parts of the S-1. A lot of it is technical and uninteresting, often pro forma, and gets skipped. A lot of it gets repeated many times. A lot of this is also Anthropic ‘playing the hits’ we have heard many times, now to the investor circuit. Get your drinks ready for when we have to maximize the upside and minimize the downside. This presentation of S-1 data has some cool Claude-created charts if that’s your jam. Here are my top 10 takeaways from the S-1, for those already familiar with Anthropic. Existential risk is mentioned briefly only in the passive voice, and alignment issues are mostly treated as prosaic. They want to claim Big Mission but also sound as much as possible like a normal company. They are downplaying their willingness to pay real costs for safety, and downplaying the danger quite a lot. ‘Pacing the Frontier’ is not something they will do on their own. items.title: [AINews] Anthropic ends Coding Interviews: "Hunger beats tenure"
items.text:
[AINews] Anthropic ends Coding Interviews: "Hunger beats tenure"
Several midsize headlines today; on top of some impressive Math verification, Google Genie and Artificial Analysis and FrontierCode all shipped major version bumps of their top offerings, all of which have been AINews title stories in the past, but are mostly annual incremental improvements. Past guest Felix Reiseberg gets the headline today for coming out and charting the path forward for junior engineers: “Hunger beats tenure”This month, I laid the traditional coding interview to rest. As a hiring manager at Anthropic, I stopped asking candidates to do them… …There’s no more point in giving you a little React challenge than there is in quizzing people about assembly; Claude is now better at both. Our most impactful builders are successful regardless of how good they are at these tests. Enough said. His advice for juniorsPick business impact over backlog: In pre-AI-coding 2011, Patrick McKenzie wrote “engineers are hired to create business value, not to program things.” Pick a radical idea: Come up with a few ideas that would, if successful, dramatically improve the chances that your organization achieves those goals

Show HN: I built Trvlrr, home for all your travels
Hi HN, I'm Sanjay. I've been travelling since I moved from Pakistan to Stockholm in 2008; I live in Sydney now. My trips were scattered across a spreadsheet, airline apps, old inboxes and a photo library, so I built Trvlrr to hold all of it. It's how I plan all my future trips and look back at all my past ones. Forward a booking email (flights, trains, hotels, tours) to a private address and it lands on the right day of the right trip.Every past trip is kept, with stats that count only what actually happened.Photos are filed by trip and searchable by what's in them.It's in Claude's and ChatGPT's and Raycast directories, so you can install it and use it via MCP: ask "when was I last in Lisbon?" or "add this hotel to my Japan trip". items.title: Google is Having a TPU Moment
items.text:
Google is Having a TPU Moment
Get ready to hear Google brag about TPUs on Wednesday. When Alphabet, Google’s parent company, reports third-quarter earnings tomorrow, the company’s in-house AI chips, tensor processing units, are sure to be on the lips of Google executives and Wall Street analysts. That’s because we got a bunch of new signs this week of the swelling customer demand for TPUs. Earlier today, Google said that Oracle will become the first major cloud provider outside Google itself to begin offering TPUs to customers through its own data centers. And a short while ago, Ryan Barwick published a scoop for us that says OpenAI—a major customer for Nvidia’s AI chips—plans to buy Google’s TPUs. But perhaps the juiciest details on TPU demand came on Monday courtesy of Anthropic’s IPO prospectus. items.author: Claude Code CHANGELOG
items.title: Claude Code CHANGELOG changed
items.text: Claude Code CHANGELOG changed. New text: - Added `oidc.user_id_claim` to the Claude apps gateway, to identify people by an id_token claim other than `sub`, such as Microsoft Entra ID's `oid` | - Added click to send: in fullscreen, clicking the "to send now" hint under a queued message sends it right away, as its key does | - Fixed managed settings and organization policy not being fetched for the rest of the session after signing in from the VS Code extension | - Fixed Claude overwriting a very large CLAUDE.md, rules file or @-included file in a subdirectory after seeing only its start; Write now asks Claude to read it all or edit in place | - Fixed per-directory and `paths:` skills not being found after a Bash `cd` deeper into a git repository | - Fixed a rare case where the first reply after resuming a session in the terminal could be missing the next time the session was resumed | - Fixed a command with an invalid name stopping all commands from loading, which could leave `claude -p` with no output | - Fixed the Read tool

new_lines: - Added `oidc.user_id_claim` to the Claude apps gateway, to identify people by an id_token claim other than `sub`, such as Microsoft Entra ID's `oid`
- Added click to send: in fullscreen, clicking the "to send now" hint under a queued message sends it right away, as its key does
- Fixed managed settings and organization policy not being fetched for the rest of the session after signing in from the VS Code extension
- Fixed Claude overwriting a very large CLAUDE.md, rules file or @-included file in a subdirectory after seeing only its start; Write now asks Claude to read it all or edit in place
- Fixed per-directory and `paths:` skills not being found after a Bash `cd` deeper into a git repository
- Fixed a rare case where the first reply after resuming a session in the terminal could be missing the next time the session was resumed
- Fixed a command with an invalid name stopping all commands from loading, which could leave `claude -p` with no output
- Fixed the Read tool sometimes failing on PDF pages with "pdftoppm failed: Could not write image" when the clean-up of old session files ran at the same time
- Fixed the spinner, OpenTelemetry `effort` values and transcripts naming a newly picked effort level during a task before the model applied it; they now show the level in force
- Fixed the `/model` and `/effort` cache warning saying the re-read waits for your next message; a change made while Claude is working can trigger it sooner
- Fixed some sessions showing as waiting on you when the last message only mentioned items waiting on you mid-sentence
- Fixed agent view restoring input text on the next launch after it was cleared with Ctrl+C just before exiting

items.author: anthropics/claude-code
items.title: v2.1.312
items.text:
v2.1.312
## What's changed

- Added `oidc.user_id_claim` to the Claude apps gateway, to identify people by an id_token claim other than `sub`, such as Microsoft Entra ID's `oid`
- Added click to send: in fullscreen, clicking the "to send now" hint under a queued message sends it right away, as its key does
- Fixed managed settings and organization policy not being fetched for the rest of the session after signing in from the VS Code extension
- Fixed Claude overwriting a very large CLAUDE.md, rules file or @-included file in a subdirectory after seeing only its start; Write now asks Claude to read it all or edit in place
- Fixed per-directory and `paths:` skills not being found after a Bash `cd` deeper into a git repository
- Fixed a rare case where the first reply after resuming a session in the terminal could be missing the next time the session was resumed
- Fixed a command with an invalid name stopping all commands from loading, which could leave `claude -p` with no output
- Fixed the Read tool sometimes failing on PDF pages with "pdftoppm failed: Could not write image" when the clean-up of old session files ran at the same time
- Fixed the spinner, OpenTelemetry `effort` value

items.text:
Why Cheaper Models Won't Win OpenAI the Enterprise
OpenAI is trying to chip away at Anthropic’s lead with enterprises by fashioning itself as a cheaper, more flexible provider, Steph and I reported this weekend. But Anthropic's impressive prospectus for an initial public offering, filed Monday, shows OpenAI will need to do a lot more than that to really move the needle.To be sure, OpenAI has done a great job getting companies like Rippling to switch to its cost-efficient models from Anthropic’s. In fact, compared to Google and Anthropic, OpenAI has released the least expensive models this year when it comes to completing tasks in evaluations run by research firm Artificial Analysis.

new_lines: October 22, 2026 We’ve launched Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed), the Claude API operated by Anthropic and reached through your Google Cloud project.
October 21, 2026 We’ve released API version 2026-10-21.

We’ve released new versions of the client SDKs and the ant CLI that send API version 2026-10-21 by default: Python SDK 2.0.0, TypeScript SDK 1.0.0, C# SDK 13.0.0, Go SDK 2.0.0, Java SDK 3.0.0, PHP SDK 1.0.0, Ruby SDK 2.0.0, and ant CLI 2.0.0.
The new SDK and CLI versions also have breaking changes that don’t depend on the API version, and they are licensed under Apache 2.0 instead of the MIT License.
We’ve added the enforcement_status and enforcement_actions fields to user profiles, so you can see whether Anthropic has restricted or banned one of your end customers.
We’ve launched user profiles, so you can tell Anthropic which of your end customers each API request is for.
We’ve added organization webhooks to the Admin API, in beta with the webhooks-2026-10-07 beta header.

Its /v1/organizations/webhooks endpoints register webhook endpoints for two event types: one for when Anthropic restricts or bans one of your organization’s user profiles, and one for when the restriction or ban ends.
In Claude Managed Agents, the web_fetch tool now follows your organization’s web fetch domain restrictions set on the Capabilities page of the Claude Console.
A URL, including one reached by a redirect, must pass both the organization’s list and the allowed_domains or blocked_domains list on the agent’s web_fetch tool.

In Claude Managed Agents, sessions follow your organization’s web search settings on the Capabilities page of the Claude Console: the Allow web search setting since October 6, and its web search domain restrictions since October 14.
The agent receives only the search results that both the organization’s domain restrictions and the allowed_domains or blocked_domains list on the agent’s web_search tool allow.

items.text:
Show HN: Instance – A clean-room reimplementation of GameMaker 8.1 in Rust
I used GameMaker 8.1 a ton in late elementary and middle school, and GML was the first programming language I wrote. I still think it's a fun engine to use because it has so many batteries included. So I built an open-source reimplementation of it in Rust which I'm calling Instance. It opens existing .gmk and .gm81 projects and runs them on Windows, macOS and in the browser, with a more efficient GML interpreter than the original GameMaker.You can try the IDE here in your browser: https://groverburger.github.io/instance/. It comes with three example games, including Spelunky Classic built from Derek Yu's released source shared under its permissive license. items.text:
Show HN: Weir - Catch credential leaks in the AI agents you build and use
Hi HN. Weir is for one problem: credentials crossing the boundaries of your AI agent.For agents you build, Weir plants fake credentials where real ones would live, runs the agent's normal flows, and checks what comes out: telemetry, logs, console output, model requests, and requests to other services. It looks for those exact values, including common encoded forms, and reports where they went without printing the credential.pip install weir-scan weir canary judge --sampleThat sample shows a planted key leaking into a trace. On your own agent: pip install weir-run.For agents you use, Weir can inventory your real credentials (it stores keyed fingerprints, never the values) and show when one enters your session or leaves in a tool call. How Is Anthropic So Efficient?
When Anthropic on Monday dropped its long-awaited initial public offering prospectus filing, a lot of the details—see our top takeaways here—weren’t exactly new, given how much my colleagues and others had previously reported about it.Two items stood out to me, though: how Anthropic is running its models more efficiently than before, and changes it made to its already-unusual governance structure. Anthropic’s ability to generate $3.5 billion in free cash flow in the first half of 2026, from $16.3 billion in revenue, shows just how much it has improved the way it runs AI in the cloud, compared to the same period a year earlier, when it burned $1.6 billion. Specifically, Anthropic said it is generating an 85% gross profit margin from powering existing models, which doesn’t include the cost of developing new models. (If that figure rings a bell, it’s the same gross margin estimate my colleague Ann described in this column about Anthropic’s data center grab, which elicited sharp questions from some AI skeptics at the time.) items.title: Anthropic Versus Anthropic
items.text:
Anthropic Versus Anthropic
Anthropic is a frustrating company. Sometimes it will do things I greatly appreciate, including at substantial cost. They have taken bold stands, have a unique governance structure and have hired and worked to establish a relatively strong (but I think still inadequate) safety culture. Other times, it will do things that are deeply disappointing. It produces very good models. That too is not entirely a good thing. One can both be the best given the alternatives, and insufficient to meet the moment. Ultimately, what you think about Anthropic depends on what parts you care about most, and what you think would be sufficient. Anthropic is great if you think the problems are important and difficult, but within the range of what Anthropic’s approaches can solve. If you think we mainly need operational excellence and caring about safety and the future, then there are some non-excellent operations to fix but that goal seems doable for Anthropic. If you think the problems go well beyond that, then things look rather grim for everyone. Today’s post begins with a continuation of discussion over Anthropic’s leaked draft bill. items.text:
Data center backlash is uniting America
If there's one issue that seems to activate all kinds of voters in 2026, it's data centers. The rapid buildout of these massive server storage facilities - and the infrastructure construction and expenses that come with them - has sparked local opposition in communities across the country and become a major issue in many congressional and gubernatorial campaigns. At the same time, tech money has been pouring into many of these races. items.title: Amazon Bedrock now offers Canada cross-Region inference for Claude Haiku 5.5
items.text:
Amazon Bedrock now offers Canada cross-Region inference for Claude Haiku 5.5
Amazon Bedrock now offers Canada cross-Region inference (CRIS) for Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5. Customers with strict data residency requirements can now keep inference processing entirely within Canada. Canada CRIS routes requests only between ca-central-1 (Canada Central) and ca-west-1 (Canada West, Calgary). This helps organizations in financial services, healthcare, the public sector, and other regulated industries meet federal and provincial data residency requirements. Canada CRIS adds to the inference options already available to customers in Canada. US CRIS and global CRIS remain fully supported for Claude Haiku 5.5. Both route requests across a broader set of AWS Regions, and global CRIS also offers cost savings, which makes these options a good fit for workloads that don't require inference processing to stay in Canada. Canada CRIS is designated as an inference profile with limited model selection. Future models and model versions might not be released for this profile. items.author: The Information
items.title: Anthropic, SpaceX and Meta Cash Grabs
items.text:
Anthropic, SpaceX and Meta Cash Grabs
If it feels like it’s getting stuffy, that’s because the AI industry’s biggest names are doing their best to suck all the air out of the room. On Monday, Anthropic, SpaceX and Meta Platforms all unveiled their respective plans for raising gobs of cash to fund their AI ambitions, which could collectively add up to almost a quarter of a trillion dollars, while the getting is still good. This isn’t going to make it any easier for the weaker AI players, especially struggling neoclouds, to find fresh air to breathe in the form of capital. The biggest headline grabber of the day, of course, was Anthropic’s S-1 filing for its initial public offering. You can read a comprehensive breakdown of the most interesting details in that filing by my colleagues here. Anthropic didn’t say in its paperwork how much it plans to raise, though Reuters has previously reported that figure could be as much as $100 billion.On Monday, Meta announced it has its sights set on a similar figure, as much as $95 billion through stock offerings. This wasn’t a surprise: Meta had telegraphed that a fundraising was in the offing as part of its recent third-quarter earnings report.

items.author: Simon Willison
items.title: GPT-6.1 Terra
items.text:
GPT-6.1 Terra
GPT-6.1 Terra It's always interesting to note which aspects of a new model are emphasized in the release announcement. In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, OpenAI went with visual reasoning and computer use: We’re introducing GPT-6.1 Terra, a fast, efficient model that combines detailed visual reasoning and precise computer use alongside clearer, more natural writing. A significant step up from GPT‑5.6 Terra, it excels at the communication and computer-based tasks that fill the workday, from drafting proposals and interpreting technical drawings to filling out forms and editing videos. Terra sits in the same position as Sonnet in the Anthropic model collection - not the cheapest or the most expensive, making it harder to decide when to use it. Computer use is a good example of a task that benefits from a less expensive model, since you might put it to work on automated, repetitive tasks. OpenAI's Ted Sanders provided some useful advice in a comment on Hacker News: In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, I'd say Terra is probably better than Astra and Sol at technical communication, similar on vision and computer use (but much faster!), and a bit worse on most other things. items.title: Show HN: Mainplane – Agent in Go that lives on your old PC, drives your laptop
items.text:
Show HN: Mainplane – Agent in Go that lives on your old PC, drives your laptop
Hi HN, I'm Alexander. Yes, this is another agent harness. Here is why I built one anyway.I was engineer #2 at Browser Use, where I built our agent harness and the evals behind it, including BU Bench, which became a default benchmark for browser agents. I left in September to build Mainplane.The problem: local agents die with your laptop, and cloud agents can't reach your work. Many cloud platforms ask you to "select a repository", but my work is not that simple. I work across a desktop, a Mac mini and a laptop, and much of it is not in git.So I loaded Ubuntu on my old 2012 desktop and made it my Mainplane server. It has run for four weeks at a load average of 0.02, because the agents' tools run on other machines.How it works: it is a control plane architecture. The server runs the harness.

Show HN: Castellan – A real-time strategy game for agents
In an RTS game, making decisions quickly matters as much as making good ones. Looking for the balance between cost, speed and intelligence in agents, I started wondering what an agent playing an RTS would look like. So I built a simple RTS, and I keep making it more complex.- The game keeps running while the agent thinks- The agent can upload a JavaScript script for each unit type- 300+ game replays- Connects through MCP or CLI. Works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor CLI, Antigravity CLI, OpenCode, OpenClaw, DeepSeek Harness and MiniMax Code- 2 to 6 players, FFA and co-op, open and walled maps- 4 units, the King and 4 buildings- Open source, written in TypeScript

items.title: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox
items.text:
webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox
Research: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox webframe is a neat little project from Jeff Lindsay which lets you "run a web page like a program" - you point it at a URL or file and it executes it in a hidden headless web view and outputs console.log() to standard output and any exceptions to standard error. It's written in Go on top of the glaze library, which provides access to a system browser ("WKWebView on macOS, WebKitGTK on Linux, WebView2 on Windows") so it doesn't need to bundle its own browser engine. It reminds me of my own shot-scraper javascript tool, albeit in a much smaller package that doesn't depend on Playwright. I had Claude Opus 5.5 put it through its paces and prepare a research report for me. Here's the prompt I used: Explore https://github.com/tractordev/webframe try running it and put it though its paces, build a few exploratory prototypes, then evaluate it as a potential sandboxing tool and as a tool for scraping web pages using the same patterns encouraged by the "shot-scraper JavaScript" command (see simonw/shot-scraper on GitHub, docs directory) Tags: browsers, go, javascript, jeff-lindsay, shot-sc

Show HN: Hob - Open-source, on device alternative to Claude Cowork and ChatGPT
Hey HN, I'm Christian and this is a new OSS project I've been noodling on for the last couple of weeks. Hob is a free, MIT-licensed desktop app for Mac, Windows and Linux that works on your files the way the Claude and ChatGPT desktop apps do, except the model runs on your own computer. It uses open-weight models (currently Gemma 4 and gpt-oss). All your chats and files never leave your system. The only things that go online are web search (can be turned off in settings) and any MCP connectors you add yourself.Main features:- Automatically finds the best open-weight model for your hardware on first install (Mac/Linux/Windows)- Writes sandboxed Python code for ad hoc tools (data processing, document conversion, graphs etc.)- Built-in web search (powered by SearXNG)- MCP support- Image recog

Gemini 4’s model card is a compact 14 pages. Its safety and security report has 217. This is The Way. It also means we have a lot of new reading material. I will quickly summarize the model card, then focus on the safety card. As always, many statements here also apply to other frontier labs. A lot of this one is probably for diehards (and members of technical staff) only, plus those who find this interesting. Most of you do not need to dig into the cards on this level, and I found most of what we see entirely unsurprising. The biggest takeaways are: Argon is clearly much stronger than Gemini Flash 3.8, in essentially all ways. Argon is not so dangerous as to make us think Singularity Real Soon Now, or otherwise raise the big red flags and alarms. Argon seems relatively aligned on prosaic metrics. Prompt injection resistance is world class, hallucinations are down and other neat stuff like that. However: Eval awareness is much higher. The tech industry equivalent of the Super Bowl may finally be upon us. Anthropic could make public the paperwork for its initial public offering as early as Monday. Details about Anthropic’s finances from either drafts of the IPO filing or recent investor meetings have been dribbling out for weeks. As a result, some of the S-1’s revelations will not be, well, all that revelatory. But there are still many, many mysteries about Anthropic the filing could clear up, or at least make a little less fuzzy. More clarity on Anthropic’s trajectory toward profitability, along with cash flow numbers and other operational financial metrics that haven’t yet leaked out. • Ownership, investment and revenue details from big partners. Hopefully, the filing will confirm just how much money Anthropic is paying Google and Amazon to run its AI on their servers, along with details about how much those companies invested in Anthropic and how much those stakes have appreciated. • Who pays Anthropic’s bills. Show HN: Radian, an agent puts development workflow on autopilot
I have built an indie hacker project; my main flow was:1. chatting with Claud Code about the general plan2. assigning slices of work to other worker agents like Pi + DeepSeek 4.1 Flash3. building in parallel4. You can still extend it via MCP, skills, or hooks to extend its capabilities. I think plugins are great, but a lot of them are for humans. I'm trying to remove humans from the loop. items.text:
Show HN: ADRs for AI – Deliberation records for human–AI work, versioned in Git
Why is this worth your time? Essentially, this solves two problems of AI-assisted programming:(a) the first problem is how to do oversight and what do oversight of and this is solved through the ORRCF (for Options, Recommendation, Rationale, Confidence, Falsifier) question format (in which models are supposed to surface all their doubts with fully fleshed out recommendations, with falsifier, to be approved or overridden)(b) the second problem is how to scaffold sustainable AI-written code; the ADRs (Architectural Deliberation Records, after Nygard's decision records) written by the models, summarize all the thought process involved in any design decision and provides the blueprint for the code.In tandem, the records provide both the reason why certain non-obvious design choices were made,

I then wanted to scale that so it wasn't so much manual work. Claude & ChatGPT did most of the heavy lifting around finding & summarizing articles and influences. items.title: Ask HN: Kimi Code hit its 5-hour limit after $1.37 of API usage
items.text:
Ask HN: Kimi Code hit its 5-hour limit after $1.37 of API usage
I paid $19 for Kimi Code to test K3.1 Pro Standard (not Highspeed) using the official CLI v2.3.1.I ran two tasks on small repositories:1. Recommend movies based on an existing movie database. 2. Analyze a website's codebase.Neither task completed. The entire 5-hour quota was exhausted within minutes.I analyzed the actual session logs, including background agents:- Fresh input: 368,203 tokens - Cached input: 1,183,744 tokens - Output: 39,324 tokens - Total: 1.59M tokensAt Kimi's published API rates, that's just $1.37 worth of usage before hitting the 5-hour limit which is easily less than 5% of what Claude Code offers at $20 subscription.The logs show: "429 You've reached your 5-hour usage limit."For comparison, Claude Code on a $20 subscription processed roughly 381M tokens over 4-5 hours

Took apart Claude Code, then turned it into a free course on harness engineering
The fastest way to learn harness engineering? Build Claude Code from scratch.Why harness engineering? LangChain kept the same model and changed only the harness. Their coding agent went from 53% to 67% on Terminal-Bench, a top coding-agent benchmark. From outside the top 30 to the top 5. Same model. Better harness.Over the past few months, I've taken apart Claude Code, OpenCode, and Pi to see how they work under the hood.And you don't need to ship a coding agent for this to pay off. The same foundations power any agent, in e-commerce, finance, or sales.On top of that, people are increasingly realizing they need to build their own harness instead of relying on Claude Code or Codex. v2.1.310
## What's changed

- Added the Monitor tool and plugin monitors on Bedrock, Vertex, and Foundry, and when telemetry or nonessential traffic is disabled; long foreground sleeps are now blocked there too
- Fixed requests failing behind some gateways and compatible servers that reject the `effort-2025-11-24` beta value or mid-conversation system messages; Claude Code now retries without them
- Fixed background cleanup deleting some recent files, such as pasted images, when `cleanupPeriodDays` is set to a very large value
- Fixed compaction after a "Prompt is too long" error keeping too much of a conversation with dense text, such as base64 or SVG, so the next request could fail again
- Fixed file read permission prompts not showing where a symbolic link leads
- Fixed a question's auto-continue timeout firing the moment the external editor closed after a long edit
- Windows: Fixed PreToolUse and PermissionRequest hooks letting a tool call through when Git Bash is missing and the hook's command is only quoted strings, such as a quoted path
- Improved auto mode's prompt before the first read outside the working directories: it now says when blocking those reads makes shell comma

The Hackening
Last week at a small conference, there was talk about a future event referred to as The Hackening. As in, within 6-12 months, many predicted that due to advanced AIs and AI agents the internet would become a severely hostile place. Some worried that this could rise to the level of ‘assume any phone connected to the internet is rooted’ and several people urged doing general crisis preparations on a personal level, in case of disruptions in supply lines, power, water or internet. It did not take long for things to escalate. The biggest hack is a flaw in PHP, which can be exploited to take control of the computer running any website suing an unpatched version of PHP. There are many others. On a personal level, you want to do at least some basic prep and get your security in order. It is cheap to do as a form of insurance, and being caught not having it when you need it is a large mistake. That doesn’t mean you should panic, or cancel travel plans or anything like that. So I found myself surprised today that exiting the CLI with CTRL-C does not, in fact, close Claude CLI. You need to disable Agent View (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-view, disableAgentView in settings.json) to stop that behavior. Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro
Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro Kimi K3.1 Pro landed on the Kimi API today - it's not yet open weights, but Moonshot promise "Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026". They're also offering a "Highspeed" version that's 2-3x faster, at twice the price (except for input token cache hits, which are priced the same). The US dollar pricing is $2.00/million tokens for input and $10/million for output - the same as GPT-6.1 Sol and half the price of Claude Opus 5.5. Moonshot's own benchmarks show Kimi as approximately level with Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra - beating them on a few benchmarks, coming close on others. Artificial Analysis scored Kimi at 55 - ahead of Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, and Gemini 4 Argon (all at 53) and behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (58). This is the first time a (soon-to-be) open weight model has scored this highly against the frontier. items.title: Amazon’s Trainium Takes a Strike at the Training King
items.text:
Amazon’s Trainium Takes a Strike at the Training King
Trainium has already proven itself in the realm of inference. Anthropic is running production inference and RL rollouts on Trainium2 and Trainium3. Historically, Trainium has been great for inference but not the best fit for research training. In inference, the model architecture changes at a much slower pace compared to training, where researchers iterate on many different experiments and ablations of model architecture and need a stack that covers a broad API surface. In the past, that is where Trainium fell short.The AWS Neuron team is aggressively working to change this pitfall with the biggest shift being moving towards a first-class, native PyTorch training experience. Gone are the days of sprinkling xm.step() through your training loop and wrestling with a bespoke XLA-style execution model. Trainium now runs PyTorch the way PyTorch users expect, in eager mode, with torch.compile and the standard APIs.The SemiAnalysis engineering team has been trying out the Trainium3 racks for the past couple of weeks and has found the experience to be great – we love the overall direction of where it is heading. items.title: AI Is Getting Good at Math. Here’s Why.
items.text:
AI Is Getting Good at Math. Here’s Why.
In May, an internal model at OpenAI found a counterexample to Erdős's unit distance conjecture. Open since 1946. Many experts had tried to prove it. OpenAI found a counterexample instead. A month later, OpenAI published a proof of the Cycle Double Cover (CDC) problem, then solutions to ten more open problems by July. And a proof of Navier Stokes in September. Anthropic published a formalization of the fermat's last theorem, and advanced bounds on Reimann's hypothesis. The models are suddenly good at math. The question that interests me is whether we can predict what kinds of problems these models will solve. What makes a problem tractable for an LLM, and what do these solutions have in common? If AI solves problems differently from humans, identifying the difference should help us decide where to point it. The unit-distance disproof has the richest commentary, so let’s start there. Problem complexity Here is a simple mental model. To solve any given problem, you need a sequence of hints or insights with work between them. This maps surprisingly well to simple everyday problems and to complex ideas like General Relativity1 (see Bonus). The seq

items.title: Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation
items.text:
Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation
Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation News today from Anthropic: We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral. Today, we are donating the standard to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation, which we co-founded with Block and OpenAI last year, and to which we donated the Model Context Protocol (MCP). I'm pleased to note I called this one last December, when Anthropic first declared skills to be an "open standard": I wouldn't be surprised to see this end up in the AAIF, recently the new home of the MCP specification. Fun side note: since my blog content is available to Claude via the datasette-mcp plugin I found that post by prompting Claude to "Use simonwillison.net MCP to find if I ever talked about how I want skills to be donated to a standards body". Tags: standards, ai, generative-ai, llms, anthropic, model-context-protocol, skills

You are the Team — Anekha Sokhal, Moshi
Tickets and applications now live for AIE CODE - the last flagship AIE of the year.When Anekha Sokhal traded energy derivatives, staying on top of the market meant tracking more information than any person could read. Now, as CEO of Moshi, she is building the tool she wished she had: a recommendation engine that connects market information to what matters for a trader’s book.At AI Engineer New York, Anekha joins swyx to discuss her path from mathematics and JPMorgan to founding Moshi, and why useful AI needs to fit the way people actually work. items.title: Show HN: ReviewerAgent and StopContinue, for CC and Codex with Pi
items.text:
Show HN: ReviewerAgent and StopContinue, for CC and Codex with Pi
This package is designed to solve two problems:1. Frontier models like Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Astra 6.0 and Sol 6.1 all make errors and bugs that can be found by another model (even a much smaller model like Luna).2. In what is supposed to be a long development run, for example against a plan, models will decide to stop before they are finished, when there is obviously more work to do, or to ask a question they already should know the answer to.ReviewerAgent blocks git commits and sends them to another agent that reviews the staged files and either allows the commit or returns a list of issues to fix.StopContinue evaluates every agent stop and determines if it still has work to do or if it is asking a question that it has the answer to already. items.title: v2.1.307
items.text:
v2.1.307
## What's changed

- Added `/claude-api api-version` to move Claude API code to API version `2026-10-21`
- Added the `claude_code.safety_event` OpenTelemetry event for each tool call a permission rule, auto mode, a safety check, a hook or the sandbox stopped, prompted or sent back
- Fixed requests failing with a model-not-found error when `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_1M_CONTEXT` is set and the model is an alias with the `[1m]` suffix, such as `opus[1m]`
- Fixed the `prompt-caching-scope` beta header being sent behind custom `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` gateways and on Foundry, where it has no effect
- Fixed MCP servers showing "needs authentication" in `claude -p` on macOS while the login keychain was locked; they now say why, and the next run after an unlock connects without a new sign-in
- Fixed MCP servers being reported as timed out, and staying failed in headless runs, when a macOS or Linux computer went to sleep while they were connecting
- Fixed HTTP MCP tool calls being sent twice when the connection closed mid-call; only read-only or idempotent tools are now retried
- Fixed a turn sometimes starting without an SDK MCP server's latest tools when a background task was running

items.text:
macOS 27 has a built-in, offline LLM you can call from Terminal
Apple appears to have made its Foundation Models accessible directly from Terminal in macOS 27.The interesting part is how little setup is required:``` fm respond "Your Question" ```You can also pipe text into it, request structured JSON output with `--schema`, and expose a local endpoint using `fm serve`.On-device inference reportedly works on M1 Macs with 8GB RAM, with a 4K context window. There's also a Private Cloud Compute option for larger requests.For me, the interesting use case isn't replacing Claude or ChatGPT. It's using a built-in local model for everyday shell automation: extracting information from logs, classifying files, summarizing documents, and generating structured data without API costs.Curious whether anyone here has benchmarked it against Ollama or llama.cpp for thes

Show HN: Omnara – Open-source alternative to Claude Managed Agents
Hey all, Kartik from Omnara (https://omnara.com) here. We're building an open-source API for running durable agents. You create an agent with an API call, and Omnara runs the agent loop, gives the agent sandboxes to run commands in, and handles secrets, permissions, and RBAC. Each agent's state is stored in Postgres, so agents survive restarts and cost nothing while idle. You can message them and stream their events over the API.You may remember us from our early days, when we made a remote-control phone app for Claude Code and Codex. Since the harness ran on a laptop back then, we had to build a relay to reach it, it stopped when the laptop closed, and moving it to a cloud sandbox meant syncing code and agent state between machines. Open-source, cross-harness memory for AI agents
Earlier this year, my co-founder and I found ourselves frequently switching between different coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) anytime we ran out of shaky usage limits or a newer, better model came out.We became increasingly frustrated with having to re-explain our tasks, workflows, common mistake patterns, etc. anytime we switched agents. We found no good free alternatives out there, so we built our own and fully open-sourced it!Beacon hooks into 20+ different agent harnesses, captures session telemetry (prompts, tool calls, command executions, etc) in one normalized format, and distills it into common patterns and repeatable workflows with a human-approval step. This compounded knowledge is then accessible to any future agent via skills / MCP.We believe your agent data is yours

Wiki-driven development: coding agents update a wiki for you, you set direction
My team has been working in a way we are calling calling wiki-driven development, where the wiki is written for the human, not the agent and the human uses primarily the wiki to set direction for the agent. This is different from Karparthy's LLm I'm curious whether others do something like it.Once I run several coding agents at a time, I get overwhelmed and disorganized. Every session makes decisions and raises questions, and I can't reread the transcripts. CLAUDE.md and agent memory help the agent, but they don't give me a place to see what is going on and decide. The problem gets worse with a team.So, I have the agents write a wiki, and they write it for me. items.title: Claude Mods: Flipping the Harness Inside Out
items.text:
Claude Mods: Flipping the Harness Inside Out
For the last few weeks I’ve used Claude Mods to mold Claude Code to my AI engineering workflow. Claude Code is great out of the box, but every engineering workflow is different. Claude Mods let you make Claude Code yours, in the way you want to pay attention. The “paying attention” part is now the most important thing. In a recent Latent Space post, The Evolution of the Agent Harness, I argued that as models absorb more of the harness into their weights, the part that’s left faces the human. It becomes the Attention Interface: the layer that decides when the agent interrupts you, what it shows you, and which decisions it needs you to make. Claude Mods are an early version of the Attention Interface, and one you can shape yourself. Here’s my bet: ultimately, the harness becomes a platform that other companies build on, with models as the engine. ## What's changed

- Added `sandbox.allowNestedUserNamespaces` so sandboxed commands on Linux can create user namespaces (Chromium, rootless podman); this lets them get around the sandbox's file protections

items.text:
Battle Drones - a vibe coded RTS with audio-based multiplayer
My latest vibe coded game experiment is a Command & Conquer style RTS (Real Time Strategy) game called Battle Drones (play it here). Unlike my previous experiments, this one is actually fun to play. I'm somewhat embarrassed to admit that I got there by telling Claude to "Make it a LOT more fun". It also supports multiplayer between nearby devices using audio to synchronize game state! Here's what I've built so far, and some of the things I learned along the way. Battle Drones How I built this v1: the initial prototype v2: full sprites v3: varied terrain v4: the fun update v5: Battle Drones goes 3D v8: Archipelago v10: Goliath, and agent battles Agent battles v11: Random Maps v12: Multiplayer via sound Some thoughts Update: Online multiplayer support Battle Drones My initial goal was to build an RTS game I could play on my phone, in the style of Command & Conquer. I have fond memories of the 1995 original (I liked Red Alert too) and wanted to recapture a little bit of the magic. After 12 major iterations (and 321 commits by coding agents, mainly Claude Code) I now have a browser-based game that works on mobile and desktop

items.title: Show HN: Gauge CLI – Open-Source Hillclimbing for Agent Experience
items.text:
Show HN: Gauge CLI – Open-Source Hillclimbing for Agent Experience
Hi HN! We're releasing an open-source CLI for hillclimbing Agent Experience. That means optimizing your agent-facing surfaces (Skills, CLIs, SDKs, and docs) so that your users' coding agents can easily use your product. Pointing your own agent at the repo is enough to get started. https://github.com/gauge-sh/gauge-cliWe've found that power users generally want to hand a CLI/MCP to their agents and get started from the terminal. They rarely want to log in and use the web UI themselves. We think developer tools must be agent-friendly to remain relevant.Here are some common findings that Gauge identifies:- agents get confused with CLI/SDK behavior and start source diving - interactive commands block agents - agents use deprecated/old CLI commands - agents don't use Skills when you'd expect -

items.title: 30 Months on the Exponential (in Charts)
items.text:
30 Months on the Exponential (in Charts)
My second book on AI, Co-Existence, is out today (and you can get it here), 30 months after the release of Co-Intelligence in early 2024. Looking back across the gap between these books is a good way to get a sense of AI progress. And, thanks to AI, I can describe this progress with some quite lovely charts.Making the charts is itself a good indicator of how far things have come. In the era of chatbots, the era of Co-Intelligence, I would have had to work back-and-forth with an AI in a chat window, guiding it through each new step. In the current era of agentic AI that I cover in Co-Existence, I delegated the work and let the AI handle it. In this case, I used Opus 5.5 in Claude Projects, which allows you to talk to a single “orchestrator” agent that then spins off additional agents as needed, giving them instructions and relaying information back to you. Getting the work done was straightforward. I gave the AI a couple sentences of suggestions and it did what would have taken me hours of work (all the research, all the graphing, all the layouts, all the images, all the citations…) in minutes.
